title: Ch. 7 Lecture Slides

questions.prompt: According to the slides, which statement gives the standard definition of economic growth?

options.text: The ability of an economy to produce increasing quantities of goods and services
The process by which rising productivity increases the average standard of living
An increase in the price level over time
An increase in the number of workers employed in the economy

questions.explanation: The slides (following Chapter 4) call this the **standard definition of economic growth**: the ability to produce increasing quantities of goods and services. The “rising productivity raises the average standard of living” wording is the textbook's (non-standard) definition of *long-run* economic growth.

questions.prompt: The professor says the textbook's definition of long-run economic growth is non-standard, but the course uses it to avoid confusion. Which is that definition?

options.text: The ability of an economy to produce increasing quantities of goods and services
The process by which rising productivity increases the average standard of living
Any increase in real GDP lasting more than one year
Any increase in nominal GDP caused by inflation

questions.explanation: In the course, **long-run economic growth = the process by which rising productivity increases the average standard of living** (textbook Ch. 6), while **economic growth = the ability to produce increasing quantities of goods and services** (Ch. 4). Keep the two definitions separate on the test.

questions.prompt: Country M's real GDP per capita grows at 1.9% a year starting from $5,000 in 1960. Approximately what is it after 65 years (in 2025)? Use 5,000 × (1.019)⁶⁵.
questions.explanation: 1.019⁶⁵ ≈ 3.40, so 5,000 × 3.40 ≈ **$17,000**. Country G, growing at only 0.4%, reaches about $6,500. **Key point: in the long run, small differences in growth rates result in large differences in living standards.**

questions.prompt: Two countries start in 1960 with real GDP per capita of $5,000. Country G grows at 0.4% per year and Country M at 1.9% per year. By about 2025, which statement is closest to the slide's result?

options.text: Both are within $1,000 of each other, since the growth-rate difference is only 1.5 percentage points
Country G is about $11,000 and Country M about $17,000
Country M is about $17,000 and Country G about $6,500: small growth-rate differences compound into big differences in living standards
Country M is about $10,000, double its 1960 level, and Country G stays at $5,000

questions.explanation: The slides' key point: **small differences in growth rates produce large differences in living standards over the long run**. At 1.9% the level more than triples (≈ $17,000); at 0.4% it rises only about 30% (≈ $6,500).

questions.prompt: Real GDP per capita was $40,000 in one year and $41,200 the next. What was the growth rate (in %)?
questions.explanation: Growth rate = (41,200 − 40,000)/40,000 × 100 = **3.0%**: the percentage change from the previous year.

questions.prompt: Real GDP growth was 2.0% in year 1, −1.5% in year 2 and 3.1% in year 3. Using the averaging shortcut, what is the approximate average annual growth rate (in %, 1 decimal)?
questions.explanation: Average = (2.0 − 1.5 + 3.1)/3 = 3.6/3 = **1.2%**. Over a few years we approximate the annual rate by averaging the yearly growth rates.

questions.prompt: At the Industrial Revolution growth rate of about 1.8% per year, roughly how many years does it take real GDP per capita to double? Use the Rule of 70.
questions.explanation: Rule of 70: years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate = 70 ÷ 1.8 ≈ **39 years** (the slide says “roughly every 40 years”; either answer is fine).

questions.prompt: According to the slides, what must happen for real GDP per capita to increase?

options.text: The population must increase
The price level must rise
The government must increase spending
Labour productivity must increase

questions.explanation: The slides state: **increases in real GDP per capita depend on increases in labour productivity**, the quantity of goods and services produced by one worker or one hour of work. This leads to the question of what causes labour productivity to grow.

questions.prompt: Which pair of inputs does the Solow-Swan model on the slides include, and what is deliberately left out to keep things simple?

options.text: Labour (L, total hours worked) and physical capital (K); natural resources and human capital are left out of the production function
Labour and technology only; physical capital is left out
Physical capital and human capital only; labour is left out
Labour, physical capital and natural resources; technology is left out

questions.explanation: The model has **two factors of production, L (total hours worked) and K (physical capital)**. Natural resources and human capital are real inputs but are excluded to keep the model simple. (Technology A is not a factor of production here; it is in the production function.)

questions.prompt: In the Solow-Swan production function, Y = A·F(K, L), what does A represent?

options.text: Total saving in the economy
The level of technology
The capital stock
Labour productivity

questions.explanation: The production function maps the capital stock (K), labour (L) and the **level of technology (A)** into output (Y). A is not capital or labour; labour productivity is Y/L.

questions.prompt: A closed economy invests $2.5 million in a year, and capital depreciation is $0.6 million. By how many millions of dollars does the capital stock change?
questions.explanation: ΔK = investment − depreciation = 2.5 − 0.6 = **$1.9 million**. (The slide's example: I = $1,000,000 and depreciation = $100,000 raises K by $900,000.) If I equals depreciation, K stays constant.

questions.prompt: In the Solow-Swan model's capital accumulation equation, which statement is correct?

options.text: The capital stock keeps growing as long as depreciation is positive
In a closed economy, investment must be smaller than saving
If investment is smaller than depreciation, the capital stock shrinks
Depreciation adds to the capital stock

questions.explanation: ΔK = I − depreciation. **Investment adds to K; depreciation (wear and tear) subtracts from it.** If I equals depreciation, K is constant; if I is less than depreciation, K falls. In a closed economy, total saving equals investment.

questions.prompt: In the slides' growth model, how is labour productivity measured, and which of these is not one of its key determinants?

options.text: Labour productivity is Y/K; the determinants are K/L, technology and population size
Labour productivity is L/Y; the determinants are K/L, technology and inflation
Labour productivity is Y/L; the determinants are K/L, technology and the price level
Labour productivity is Y/L; the determinants are K/L, technology and human capital, and the size of the population is not one of them

questions.explanation: In the model, **labour productivity = Y/L**, and its three key determinants are the **capital-labour ratio K/L, the level of technology A, and human capital**. Population size does not appear: population growth does not by itself raise output per worker.

questions.prompt: What does the per-worker production function (Y/L against K/L) show about adding more and more capital per hour worked?

options.text: Diminishing returns: each additional unit of capital adds less to output per hour than the one before
Constant returns: each additional unit adds exactly the same amount
Increasing returns: each additional unit adds more than the one before
Output per hour eventually falls when the capital-labour ratio rises

questions.explanation: The slide says the first units of capital are the most effective; subsequent increases bring **diminishing returns**: smaller increases in output from raising one factor while the others are held constant. The curve flattens, but it does not fall.

questions.prompt: A retailer rearranges the layout of its stores and sales rise with the same inputs. A manufacturer installs new software-controlled machinery. How does the slide classify these changes?

options.text: Both are embodied technological change
The store rearrangement is disembodied technological change; the new machinery is embodied technological change
The store rearrangement is embodied; the new machinery is disembodied
Neither is technological change, because technology means only computers

questions.explanation: **Disembodied** technological change comes from reorganizing production (rearranging a factory floor or store layout). **Embodied** technological change is built into new machinery, equipment or software. The slide notes that most technological change is embodied.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would shift the per-worker production function upward rather than move the economy along it?

options.text: An increase in the capital-labour ratio K/L
An increase in investment that raises K/L
An improvement in technology or an increase in human capital
A fall in depreciation that raises K/L

questions.explanation: A change in K/L is a **movement along** the curve. **Technological change and higher human capital shift the curve up**, giving more output per hour at every level of capital per hour. The slide stresses that long-run growth in living standards requires continuous technological progress.

questions.prompt: According to the summary slide, which of the following cannot, on their own, produce long-run growth in GDP per capita?

options.text: Technological progress
Sustained growth in human capital
New growth theory's knowledge capital
Population growth and the accumulation of physical capital

questions.explanation: Long-run growth in GDP per capita **requires technological progress (or sustained growth in human capital)**. Population growth and physical-capital accumulation alone cannot do it, because of diminishing returns.

questions.prompt: What is the shortcoming of the Solow-Swan model, and which approach addresses it?

options.text: It does not explain why technology (A) grows; new growth theory, with knowledge capital, R&D and learning by doing, addresses this
It ignores physical capital; new growth theory adds capital to the model
It does not allow for diminishing returns; new growth theory adds them
It cannot explain catch-up; new growth theory explains it with higher tariffs

questions.explanation: The model treats the technology variable A as given, so it **does not explain why A grows**. The new growth theory explains technological change through **knowledge capital, research and development, and learning by doing**.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct description of Canada's growth in real GDP per person according to the slides?

options.text: In 1950–1973 growth was slower than in any earlier period
In 2006–2020 growth averaged about 0.3%, the lowest rate in the past 150 years
In 1974–1995 growth was about the same as in 1950–1973
In the mid-1990s–2005 growth fell because of information technology

questions.explanation: Postwar boom (1950–1973): faster than any earlier period. Long slowdown (1974–1995): more than 1 percentage point lower per year. Mid-1990s–2005: **IT-driven rebound**. 2006–2020: **about 0.3%, the lowest in 150 years**.

questions.prompt: Which argument would a productivity optimist most likely make about Canada's future?

options.text: Most of the easy productivity gains from the IT revolution have been exhausted
An aging population and regulation will keep growth low
Productivity is underestimated because gains in services and technology (free apps, AI, ATM-type conveniences) are not fully captured in GDP, so true productivity growth may be higher
Newer technologies mainly improve consumer experience and not labour productivity

questions.explanation: **Optimists** argue that measurement is the problem (service-sector improvements raise living standards but are not fully captured in GDP) and that AI and semiconductors may boost productivity after an adjustment period (the productivity J-curve). The other three are **pessimist** arguments.

questions.prompt: Why does the Solow-Swan model predict catch-up (convergence)?

options.text: Developing countries have a higher K/L, so capital is more productive there
Rich countries cannot use new technology, so their growth stops
Poor countries receive aid, so they must grow faster
Developing countries have a lower K/L and a lower level of technology than developed countries, so they can grow faster, and poorer countries tend to grow faster than richer ones

questions.explanation: Because of diminishing returns, capital is more productive where there is little of it, and poor countries can also adopt technologies already invented. The prediction: **poorer countries grow faster than richer countries until the gaps narrow**, as long as they share similar institutions and conditions for growth (rule of law, stability, education).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the evidence for catch-up (Figures 7.7–7.9) is supported by the slides?

options.text: Among high-income countries from 1960–2019 the poorer ones in 1960 (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong) grew fastest, but many countries overall have not been catching up
All countries in the world have been catching up since 1960
High-income countries that started richest in 1960 (Switzerland, New Zealand, United States) grew fastest
Other high-income countries have continued to catch up to the United States since 1990

questions.explanation: The model's catch-up prediction holds **among today's high-income countries** (Fig 7.7), but **many countries haven't been catching up** (Fig 7.8), and other high-income countries have **stopped catching up to the United States** (Fig 7.9).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four factors the slides give for the slow growth of many low-income countries?

options.text: Weak rule of law
Excessive government spending on infrastructure
Wars and revolutions
Poor education and health

questions.explanation: The four factors are **weak rule of law, wars and revolutions, poor education and health, and low saving and investment**. Excessive infrastructure spending is not on the list.

questions.prompt: A Canadian firm builds a new factory in Mexico, while a Canadian pension fund buys shares in a Brazilian company. How are these classified?

options.text: Both are foreign direct investment
The factory is foreign portfolio investment; the share purchase is foreign direct investment
The factory is foreign direct investment; the share purchase is foreign portfolio investment
Both are foreign portfolio investment

questions.explanation: **Foreign direct investment** occurs when a firm builds or purchases a facility in a foreign country. **Foreign portfolio investment** occurs when an individual or firm buys stocks or bonds issued in another country. Since the 1980s, openness to both has helped developing countries grow by improving access to technology and capital.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the pro-growth policies listed on the slides?

options.text: Imposing broad tariffs to protect domestic firms
Restricting foreign investment to keep technology at home
Taxing saving to raise government revenue
Strengthening property rights and the rule of law, with independent courts and reduced corruption

questions.explanation: The slides' pro-growth policies: **strengthen property rights and the rule of law, improve health and education, promote technological change (often via FDI), and encourage saving and investment** (tax-deferred savings, investment tax credits). Tariffs, restrictions on foreign investment and taxes on saving all work against growth.

description: Original exam-style questions written from Dr. Letendre's Chapter 7 slides (Solow-Swan growth model, catch-up, growth policies).
